title: Hacking of social media accounts - what the FIR should actually state
p1: Your social media account was hacked. You go to the police station and say, “My account was hacked.” But that may not tell the full story. The details in the FIR can matter far more than people realise.
p2: A common misconception is that an FIR only needs to mention that someone gained unauthorised access. In reality, the complaint should clearly describe what happened: which account was affected, when access was lost, what changed, how the victim discovered it, and what the suspected person did afterwards.
p3: For example, if the hacker changed the password, replaced the recovery email or phone number, sent messages from the account, deleted content, demanded money, or used the account to impersonate the victim, those facts should be specifically recorded. Screenshots, login alerts, emails, profile changes and relevant URLs can help establish the sequence of events. The key takeaway: an FIR should record the actual acts committed, not just the label “hacking.” That factual detail can make the complaint much clearer for investigation.
conclusion: If your social media account were hacked today, what detail would you make sure the FIR specifically recorded?
